turns.user: What's the latest stable release of Node.js?
turns.answer:
As of 11 Nov 2026, the latest stable Node.js release I could confirm is **v26.13.0 (LTS, "Lithium")**. Node.js's own release blog lists it on Oct 28, 2026.

**A security release is due today.** The Node.js project said it will release new versions of the 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x lines on or shortly after Wednesday, November 11, to fix HIGH-severity vulnerabilities. I couldn't confirm that those patched builds are out yet, so look for a version newer than 26.13.0 on nodejs.org later today.

Other details:
- **26 is now the newest major version and the main LTS line.** Node.js 26 "Lithium" has been in Active LTS since October 28, 2026, and 26.13.0 is its first LTS release. Running nvm install --lts, setup-node's lts/*, Docker's node:lts, and Vercel's default now give 26.
- **Other supported versions:** 24.x is at 24.22.2, October 28, 2026, and 22.x is at 22.23.4, October 21, 2026 (security release). Both are in Maintenance LTS.
- **Node 27 is still a test build.** It has been an Alpha since October 29, 2026; Current from April 22, 2027.
- **Node 20 and 25 are end-of-life** and are presumed affected and will not be patched.

turns.user: Compare the free tiers of Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages for a small side project.
turns.answer:
**For most small side projects, Cloudflare Pages has the most generous free tier.** Vercel Hobby is the best fit if you're building with Next.js and the project won't make money. Netlify Free is the tightest on traffic. These are the limits as of 11 Nov 2026.

**Cloudflare Pages Free**
- **Traffic:** "On both free and paid plans, requests to static assets are free and unlimited", according to Cloudflare's own docs.
- **Builds and files:** You get 500 builds per month, 1 build at a time. A site can have up to 20,000 files, and each file can be up to 25 MiB.
- **Server code:** Any server-side code (Pages Functions) is limited to 100,000 requests per day across the account, with 10 ms of CPU time per invocation.
- **Commercial use:** There's no non-commercial restriction, unlike Vercel's Hobby plan.

**Vercel Hobby**
- **Monthly allowance:** 100 GB of Fast Data Transfer, 1 million CDN requests, 1 million function invocations and 4 hours of Active CPU each month.
- **Builds:** 100 deployments per day, 1 concurrent build, and a 45-minute maximum build time.
- **Main catch:** The plan is for personal, non-commercial use only. A site you're paid to build, or one that shows ads or sells services, needs Pro at $20 per month. Asking for donations is fine.
- **Over the limit:** Vercel pauses the affected usage instead of billing you.

**Netlify Free**
- **Credits:** You get 300 credits per month. When you use them up, projects pause until the next billing cycle.
- **What uses credits:** 15 credits per production deploy, 20 per GB of bandwidth, 2 per 10,000 web requests, and 10 per GB-hour of compute. If you spent everything on one thing, that's about 20 production deploys or 15 GB of bandwidth.
- **Free extras:** Deploy previews, branch deploys, failed deploys and form submissions don't use credits. Built-in forms are a real plus.
- **Main catch:** Running out of credits takes down every site on your account, not just one, and visitors get a Site not available page until the cycle resets.

| | Cloudflare Pages | Vercel Hobby | Netlify Free |
|---|---|---|---|
| Static bandwidth | Unlimited | 100 GB/mo | About 15 GB/mo (shares credits) |
| Commercial use | Allowed | Not allowed | Not restricted |
| At the limit | Static site keeps serving | Usage paused | All sites paused |

**Which to pick:**
- **Static site or SPA:** Cloudflare Pages.
- **Next.js app with no money involved:** Vercel.
- **You want built-in forms and traffic is low:** Netlify.

None of the three will bill you on the free plan. You'd only face downtime if you go over.

The Cloudflare limits come from its own docs, and the Netlify credit rules are on its own pricing pages. Most of the exact Vercel numbers come from recent third-party guides that match each other, so check Vercel's pricing page before you commit.

setup.user: We're shortlisting CRMs for a 20-person sales team: HubSpot, Pipedrive, Salesforce, Zoho CRM and Close. Compare their per-seat pricing.
setup.answer:
As of 9 Nov 2026, **Zoho is clearly the cheapest per seat. Pipedrive comes next. HubSpot, Salesforce and Close all land around $90–$100 per seat once you reach the tier a 20-person team usually needs.** Prices below are per user per month, in USD, billed annually unless I say otherwise. One caveat: these come from recent third-party trackers, not the vendors' own pricing pages, so check them before you sign.

**Per-seat pricing by vendor**

- **Zoho CRM:** free for 3 users, then $14, $23, $40 or $52 per user per month billed annually ($20, $35, $50, $65 billed monthly). That was checked on 10 Nov 2026.
- **Pipedrive:** $14, $39, $59 or $79 per seat per month billed annually in the US, with a 14-day free trial and no free plan. Monthly billing runs $24, $49, $79 or $99. Some older guides put Premium at $49, but the newest checks show $59. Also, Pipedrive prices by country, so from India you may see a different price.
- **HubSpot Sales Hub:** $7 per seat for Starter (a new-customer price; the $20 list price is shown crossed out), $90 for Professional (list $100, annual commitment) and $150 for Enterprise. Professional also has a required one-time onboarding fee of $1,500, and Enterprise one of $3,500. Budget for list price at renewal.
- **Salesforce Sales Cloud:** Starter Suite costs $25 and Pro Suite costs $100. Sources disagree on the plans above that. A September 2026 check lists Core at $195, Advanced at $395 and Max at $550, while older guides still show $25, $100, $175, $350, and $550 under the old Enterprise/Unlimited names. Only Starter Suite can be billed monthly.
- **Close:** $9 to $139 per user per month on annual billing: Solo is $9, Essentials is $35, Growth is $99, and Scale is $139. Solo is limited to one user, so for a team the real starting point is Essentials. Calling (~$0.02/min), phone numbers (~$1 each/mo) and SMS are billed on top of every plan.

**What 20 seats cost per year (my estimate from list prices)**

The tiers below are the first ones that include automation or sequences, which most 20-person teams end up needing.

| CRM | Typical team tier | Per seat | 20 seats/year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zoho | Professional | $23 | $5,520 |
| Pipedrive | Growth | $39 | $9,360 |
| HubSpot | Professional | $90 | $21,600 + $1,500 onboarding |
| Close | Growth | $99 | $23,760 + calling usage |
| Salesforce | Pro Suite | $100 | $24,000 |

**Where the price jumps**

- **HubSpot:** sequences, workflow automation, forecasting, and custom reporting all unlock at Professional.
- **Pipedrive:** Growth is the first plan with full email sync, tracking and up to 50 automations.
- **Close:** Growth is the first tier with workflows and the dialer.
- **Salesforce:** Pro Suite sells the Web Services API as a $25 per user per month add-on (from a source about three months old).

At 20 seats you have room to negotiate. One analyst's advice for Salesforce: past 25 seats, treat list as the opening number and negotiate from there.

setup.user: What's the cheapest paid plan on Supabase and what does it include?
setup.answer:
As of 3 Nov 2026, Supabase's cheapest paid plan is **Pro**, starting at **$25/month per organization**. The next tier up, Team, starts at $599/month. The plans are Free ($0), Pro (from $25 per organization/month), Team (from $599 per organization/month) and Enterprise (custom).

**What Pro includes:**
- 100,000 monthly active users, 8 GB of disk per project, 250 GB of egress plus 250 GB of cached egress, 100 GB of file storage, 2 million Edge Function invocations, 5 million Realtime messages, daily backups kept for 7 days and $10 a month of compute credits
- Projects stay on. Pro removes the seven-day inactivity pause that Free has, and adds email support.
- Unlimited active projects. Free is capped at 2.
- Spend caps are on by default, which blocks surprise overage bills. One source notes that the spend cap does not cover compute.

**The catch is that $25 is a starting price:**
- The $10 compute credit covers your first project's Micro instance. Every project after that pays for its own compute. For example, two Micro projects come to $35/month before usage.
- If you go over the included amounts, you pay per unit. Examples: $0.00325 per extra user, $0.125 per GB of database disk, $0.09 per GB of egress.
- Add-ons cost extra, for example a custom domain at $10 a month.
- Supabase only bills monthly. There's no annual discount on its pricing page.

All of this comes from third-party pricing guides published in the last 1–2 months, not Supabase's own pricing page. They all give the same numbers, but check supabase.com/pricing before you pay.

setup.user: Which managed Postgres hosting is cheapest for a small app: Neon, Supabase, or AWS RDS?
setup.answer:
Neon is cheapest for a small app. It costs $0 if you stay inside its free tier, and a few dollars a month on its paid plan if your app is often idle. If the database has to run 24/7, a small AWS RDS instance (about $14/month) usually beats both. Supabase Pro costs the most for the database alone ($25), but it also includes auth, storage and APIs. Prices below are as of 3 Nov 2026.

| | Free option | Cheapest paid setup | Catch |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Neon** | $0 with no credit card: 100 projects, each with 100 CU-hours and 1 GB of storage | Launch plan: $0.106 per CU-hr, $0.35 per GB-month. No monthly minimum, so a project that consumes $3 of resources is billed $3 | Usage-based, so the bill can vary month to month |
| **Supabase** | Two free projects with a 500 MB database, but free projects pause after one week of inactivity | Pro: $25 plan + $10 compute - $10 credit = $25/month for one Micro instance (1 GB RAM) | You pay a flat $25 even with low traffic |
| **AWS RDS** | New accounts get Free Tier credits on a Free plan lasting up to 6 months | db.t4g.micro with 20 GB storage in us-east-1: $13.98/mo | Only 1 GB RAM. Making it highly available (Multi-AZ) doubles the price. You set up and run more of it yourself |

**What decides it:**
- **Does your app sit idle a lot?** Neon shuts down compute when it's not in use: idle databases scale to zero, so they don't add compute cost; storage is still billed. One review notes the difference isn't your data, it's whether your app ever sleeps. Watch out for background traffic like health checks, which can keep compute awake and negate the savings.
- **Does it run all day?** This is my own calculation from Neon's rates: the smallest Neon compute (0.25 CU) running 24/7 comes to about $19/month before storage, and 1 CU comes to about $77. That's more than RDS's ~$14.
- **Do you also need auth, file storage or realtime?** Supabase's $25 includes those. CloudZero argues that for a small app this undercuts comparable managed Postgres on AWS once you count what's bundled.
- **Are you in India?** RDS costs a bit more in Mumbai. A third-party tracker lists db.t4g.micro there at $15/month on-demand, before storage.

Neon and Supabase figures come from Neon's own pricing page and recent third-party trackers. The RDS numbers come from third-party breakdowns of AWS list prices, not AWS's own page, so check the AWS calculator for your region before you commit.

turns.user: Is GPT-4 still the newest OpenAI model?
turns.answer:
No. GPT-4 is several generations old. As of 11 Nov 2026, OpenAI is on its GPT-6 family.

**Newest releases**
- **GPT-6 Cyber (5 Nov 2026)** is OpenAI's most recent model. It's for investigating vulnerabilities, reproducing them in authorized test environments, and verifying fixes, and an organization needs approval through OpenAI's Daybreak program before it can call it.
- **GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst and Flare (4 Nov 2026)** are image models, not chat models.
- **GPT-6.1 Terra (26 Oct 2026)** is the newest general-purpose model, offering visual reasoning, computer use, and writing at $1 input and $5 output per million API tokens.

**The main GPT-6 lineup**
GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI's most capable general-purpose model in the family. GPT-6.1 Sol approaches Astra on several evaluations at lower cost, while GPT-6 Luna is the fastest and least expensive GPT-6 model. Astra came out on 3 Sep 2026, and Sol and Luna followed on 22 Sep.

**How it got from GPT-4 to here**
Since GPT-4, OpenAI has released the GPT-5.x series. That includes GPT-5.4 (March 2026), GPT-5.5 (April 2026) and GPT-5.6 (June to August 2026).

These dates come from independent release trackers and roundups, not OpenAI's own site. Several of them say they're based on OpenAI's official changelog, and they all agree with each other.
